result.markdown: # Variables ![](/images/boxes.png){style="width:200px; background: white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} The output/result of a command can be saved as a __variable__. This is very useful as we can then quickly reuse the __variable__ multiple times after it has been asisgned. ## Variable assignment ![](/images/r_assignment.png){style="width:200px; border-radius:5px; background: white; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} Below is the format for creating a __variable__ in R (don't type this into R). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} variable_name <- variable_object ``` ::: There are 3 parts to the above: - The __variable name__ (`variable_name`) - This is the name of the __variable__ and is what will be used to refer to the __variable__ in future commands - `<-` is called the assignment __operator__ - It assigns the __variable object__ to the __variable name__ - Tip you can press 'ALT'+ '-' after a __variable name__ as a shortcut for the assignment __operator__ - The __variable object__ (`variable_object`) - This can be many different objects including the output/results from commands, strings/words, numbers, and many other R data types ::: {.callout-tip} ## Variable name rules **Variable** names can almost be anything. However, **Variable** names: - Must start with a letter - Cannot contain spaces - Cannot start with a number - Cannot share the same name as a command or __function__ in R - Are case sensitive - The __variable__ name `BB` is different to the __variable__ name `bb` which is different again to `bB` - I find it easiest to keep __variable names__ in lower case (more info in [R conventions page](/tips_tricks/conventions.qmd)) ::: ## Box analogy ![](/images/box.png){style="width:150px; border-radius:5px; background: white; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} A __variable__ can be thought of as a box. The __variable object__ is held in the box but it can be replaced with any other object. The __variable name__ can then be thought as the label on the box so you can tell which box is which. ## Roman numeral examples ![](/images/roman_numeral.png){style="width:300px; border-radius:5px; background: white; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} Type the below commands into the RStudio __console__. ::: {.callout-note} Remember the amount of spaces between __operators__ and __integers__ does not matter. I encourage you to experiment with this spacing so you find what is best for you in terms of ease and clarity. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bakers_dozen <- 13 kilobyte <- 1024 I <- 1 II <- I + 1 V <- 7 - II X <- (II / I) * V L <- X * V ``` ::: In the above commands the __variables__ are not printed out to the screen, this is as it should be. The __variables__ are appearing in the __environment__ pane (Top right). This is very convenient to see what __variables__ are currently in the __environment__ and to see what they contain. ## Printing out variables ![](/images/printing_press.png){style="width:150px; border-radius:5px; background: white; border: white solid 5px" fig-align="center"} To print the contents of a __variable__ to screen you can type the __variable name__ into the __console__ and press enter. This will print the __variable object__ to the screen. This is not needed for small __variable objects__, for which you can look at the __environment__ pane, but is useful for larger __variable__ **objects**. Print out the object within the `L` ____variable____. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} L ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
